abstract.p: This study addresses the strategic engineering management challenge of balancing short-term farm economic profitability with long-term soil carrying capacity restoration in staple crop systems. It aims to evaluate policy trade-offs and inter-agency coordination mechanisms across the Triple Bottom Line (TBL) dimensions—People, Planet, and Profit—to enhance regional rice food security in East Java, Indonesia. A system dynamics (SD) simulation model was engineered using STELLA software, integrating demographic demand, biophysical soil degradation/regeneration loops, farmer financial investment flows, and policy execution dynamics. Model parameters were calibrated using empirical historical data (2021–2025) and stakeholder interviews ($N$ = 45). Structural validity was evaluated through dimensional consistency, extreme-condition tests, and mean relative error (E1), defined as the average percentage deviation between simulated and historical behavior (E1 $\leq$ 4.73%). Four policy intervention scenarios were simulated over a 2026–2030 horizon: Baseline, Economic Intervention, Environmental Intervention, and a Combined Policy Intervention. The Baseline scenario experiences saturation after 2028, with the Sustainable Rice Food Security Index (SFSI) declining to 70.41 by 2030 due to unmitigated soil health degradation. The Economic Intervention scenario enhances immediate farmer profitability (SFSI = 75.43), but performance levels off over time due to ongoing biophysical soil depletion. The Environmental Interventio scenario restricting subsidized chemical fertilizer to 1,034,209 tons/year and transitioning to organic inputs exhibits steady ecological resilience (SFSI = 77.61). The Combined Policy Intervention scenario achieves the highest projected performance (SFSI = 81.12), buffering short-term financial transition shocks while supporting soil carrying capacity restoration. Overall, the simulation results suggest that biophysical soil health restoration constitutes a primary structural leverage point preventing limits-to-growth system degradation. Successful policy execution requires an integrated inter-agency roadmap: the National Food Agency must align price floors, the Ministry of Agriculture must reallocate chemical subsidies toward bio-organic supply chains and extension training, and the Ministry of Environment and Forestry must enforce regional soil organic monitoring.

sec.title: 1. Introduction
sec.p: Rice is a critical staple crop essential for fulfilling global dietary requirements [1]. In Asian rural populations, including Indonesia, rice serves as the primary staple food contributing up to 70% of daily caloric intake, while national food security strategies also emphasize local cereal diversification to complement primary supply [2]. Consequently, ensuring a stable, sufficient rice supply serves as a primary national security benchmark [3]. However, modern agricultural management faces complex, intertwined systemic pressures [4], [5]. Expanding population growth drives continuous demand expansion [6], colliding directly with finite natural resources, environmental degradation, and shifting climate patterns [7]. Food security governance must therefore transcend traditional volume-oriented stocking strategies [8] to embrace long-term sustainability frameworks [9], [10].

In sustainable agricultural engineering management, staple crop production must be evaluated across the three Triple Bottom Line (TBL) pillars: People (social), Planet (environmental), and Profit (economic) [11]. From the social perspective, food security relies on equitable public purchasing power and protecting smallholder farmer livelihoods across vulnerable supply chains [12], [13]. From the environmental perspective, conventional intensive farming frequently exceeds ecological carrying capacities, resulting in agricultural land conversion [14], irrigation stress [15], biophysical soil health degradation from excessive agrochemical inputs [13], and elevated carbon footprints [16]. Economically, farming enterprises must maintain financial efficiency and local economic viability [17]. Single-dimensional policy interventions inevitably create unintended negative externalities across non-targeted TBL dimensions over time.

Because cause-and-effect relationships within agricultural systems involve non-linear feedback loops, multi-year time delays, and accumulative stock dynamics, traditional linear modeling techniques are inadequate [1], [18]. Exogenous economic interventions (Profit) alter social adoption capacity (People) and induce non-linear biological soil reactions (Planet). To capture these dynamic complexities, system dynamics (SD) offers a rigorous methodology [19]. SD models explicit feedback structures, projects systemic trajectories over multi-year horizons, and enables risk-free policy scenario testing prior to real-world implementation [20].

From an engineering management standpoint, the central operational challenge facing decision-makers is resolving the policy execution conflict and inter-agency coordination barrier between short-term farm revenue protection (managed by the Ministry of Agriculture and the National Food Agency) and long-term biophysical soil carrying capacity preservation (governed by the Ministry of Environment and Forestry). While prior studies have applied SD to food security [21], [22] or evaluated livestock systems [23], comprehensive mathematical SD frameworks that couple biophysical soil carbon regeneration equations with economic TBL indices for staple crops remain sparse. Building upon our foundational multi-subsystem SD architecture established in dairy supply chains [23], this study completely re-engineers structural formulations to model soil organic matter dynamics, chemical fertilizer degradation loops, land cropping constraints, and paddy-to-rice milling conversion ratios.

The primary objective of this study is to design, validate, and simulate a TBL-based SD model to evaluate policy scenarios for sustainable rice food security in East Java, Indonesia. East Java represents an ideal regional scope as it serves as one of Indonesia’s primary rice-producing provinces, characterized by high production volumes and substantial regional consumption [24], while simultaneously serving as Indonesia's principal grain basket facing intense land-use conversion pressures [14], climate vulnerability [25], and persistent soil organic matter depletion [26]. The resulting model provides regional agricultural planners with an interactive decision-support platform to optimize policy sequencing, balance subsidy allocations, and align multi-agency sustainability strategies.

sec.title: 2. Literature review
sec.p: The evaluation of staple food systems requires an integrated understanding of multi-dimensional interactions across social equity, environmental ecology, and supply chain economics. While traditional agricultural modeling has relied heavily on econometric regressions and static optimization techniques, these linear approaches fail to capture the feedback delays, accumulation thresholds, and non-linear dynamics inherent in tropical agro-ecosystems. Consequently, researchers have increasingly adopted SD and TBL frameworks to evaluate supply chain sustainability.

In the domain of agricultural TBL modeling, Elyasi and Teimoury [11] applied a qualitative meta-methodology to examine sustainable rice supply chains in Iran, illustrating the soft systemic interactions between stakeholder governance and environmental compliance. Similarly, Narassima et al. [17] developed a multi-staged TBL framework combined with Multi-Criteria Decision Making (MCDM) to evaluate processing efficiency and waste reduction in Asian rice mills. However, both studies focused primarily on qualitative mapping or static operational stages, lacking continuous differential equations to project multi-year biophysical soil feedback mechanisms onto crop productivity.

Addressing dynamic systemic complexity, Papanicolaou et al. [19] engineered a comprehensive SD framework to model economic, environmental, and social trade-offs in Midwestern U.S. agroecosystems undergoing transitions from row-crop agriculture to mixed farming. While their work demonstrated the efficacy of SD in evaluating soil quality and farm revenue, their structural parameters were calibrated for temperate climate regimes and large-scale mechanized farming, rendering their equations inapplicable to tropical smallholder rice systems in Southeast Asia. sec.p: In our previous research [23], we established an overarching multi-subsystem SD integration architecture to optimize livestock supply chains, validating systemic behavior using statistical error protocols (E1, E2). However, staple crop agriculture exhibits fundamentally distinct biophysical mechanisms compared to livestock systems. Livestock models center on herd demography, mortality curves, milk yield kinetics, and feed conversion ratios. In contrast, staple rice production requires explicit mathematical formulations for biophysical soil organic matter depletion, chemical fertilizer acidification penalties, biological recovery time lags, land cropping intensity constraints, and the milling yield ratio from paddy to rice. This study retains the systemic multi-subsystem coupling logic and validation protocol of Murnawan and Purnomo [23] while building entirely new structural formulations tailored to tropical crop agronomy and Southeast Asian subsidy governance.

sec.title: 3. Methodology
sec.p: Building upon established multi-subsystem SD modeling procedure [23], this study combines qualitative causal modeling and quantitative stock-and-flow formulation within STELLA software to capture complex cause-and-effect dynamics [27]. The modeling process follows five structured stages: data parameterization, boundary definition, mathematical formulation, structural/behavioral validation, and scenario sensitivity analysis.

sec.title: 3.1. Data collection and parameter calibration
sec.p: For qualitatively abstract parameters, primary data were collected through semi-structured stakeholder interviews conducted between October 2025 and January 2026. A purposive sampling procedure was used to select 45 domain experts across key agricultural districts in East Java (Mojokerto, Jombang, Nganjuk, and Lamongan), comprising:
• 25 lead farmers and managers from active agricultural cooperatives
• 10 regional agricultural extension officers
• 10 senior officials from the East Java Department of Agriculture and Regional Food Security Agency

sec.title: 3.2. System definition and boundaries
sec.p:
The operational boundaries encompass the complete rice production value chain in East Java over a 5-year simulation horizon (2026–2030) with a numerical integration step (
Δ t
= 0.25 years). The model couples four interdependent subsystems:
• People subsystem (social): Manages human demography, birth/mortality dynamics, per capita consumption (PCC) trends, and labor participation in agricultural extension training.
• Planet subsystem (environmental): Governs soil biophysical health dynamics, chemical fertilizer acidification penalties, organic matter restoration rates, and land productivity limits.
• Profit subsystem (economic): Models farmer enterprise revenues, unit production costs, net profit accumulation, organic investment capability, and financial independence.
• Policy and Sustainable Rice Food Security Index (SFSI) subsystem: Integrates normalized outputs across TBL dimensions into the composite SFSI.

sec.title: 3.3. Qualitative modeling (causal loop diagram)

caption.title: Causal loop diagram of the Triple Bottom Line-based sustainable rice food security model

sec.p: System behavior is governed by three primary feedback loops:

• Balancing economic loop (B1): Increased harvest capacity expands rice supply, exerting downward market pressure on selling prices, which moderates profit growth and prevents excessive market overproduction.

• Reinforcing soil degradation loop (R1): Heavy CFU accelerates biophysical soil organic matter depletion (soil degradation). Decreasing soil health reduces crop yields, driving farmers to apply additional chemical fertilizers to meet short-term targets, further degrading long-term soil health.

• Reinforcing ecological recovery loop (R2): Elevated farmer profits enable higher reinvestment in organic fertilizers (organic investment capability). Organic applications accelerate soil regeneration, restoring soil health, boosting yield capacity naturally, and strengthening future enterprise profits.

sec.title: 3.4. Quantitative modeling (stock and flow diagram)
sec.p: The stock and flow diagram (SFD) represents a formal stage for transforming the CLD conceptual model into a quantitative model incorporating mathematical formulations [27], [30]. Within the social aspect of the SD model, the primary stock variable is the human population; this is driven by BRs and MRs, which in turn influence PCC and total rice demand. This leads to the emergence of a specific stock within the economic aspect—namely, farmer profit—which is driven by the rate of profit growth and the level of investment, thereby influencing financial self-sufficiency. Finally, regarding the environmental aspect, the primary stock is soil health, which is determined by the rates of soil regeneration and degradation. Figure 2 illustrates the quantitative SFD layout.

sec.title: 3.6. Scenario development
sec.p: Four policy scenarios were evaluated over the 2026–2030 simulation horizon:
• Scenario 1 (Baseline): Continuation of existing agricultural trends without policy changes (CFU = 1,723,682 tons/year, Price = IDR 12,000,000/ton, Subsidy = IDR 500,000/ton).

• Scenario 2 (Economic Intervention): Implementation of updated price floors under National Food Agency Regulation No. 04/2024 [32], combined with an author-assumed effective unit subsidy proxy of IDR 640,000/Ton. This proxy value serves as an assumed operational parameter for policy simulation—derived by dividing estimated regional budget allocations by physical quotas under Ministry of Agriculture Regulation No. 01/2024 [33], rather than an officially prescribed regulatory subsidy rate.

• Scenario 3 (Environmental Intervention): An author-defined assumption capping chemical fertilizer use at a 40% restriction level (CFU = 1,034,209 tons/year), supported by empirical findings from Han et al. [34] regarding partial chemical fertilizer substitution with bio-organic inputs to optimize yield and reduce greenhouse gas emissions.
• Scenario 4 (Combined Policy Intervention): Simultaneous implementation of economic price supports (Scenario 2) and environmental organic transitions (Scenario 3).

sec.title: 4.2. Policy scenario simulation trajectories (2026–2030)
sec.p: Simulation trajectories for the composite SFSI across all four scenarios are summarized in Table 4 and illustrated in Figure 3.

caption.title: Simulated Sustainable Rice Food Security Index trajectories (2026–2030)
Simulation trajectories of the Sustainable Rice Food Security Index under scenarios 1–4

sec.p: Under Scenario 1 (Baseline), SFSI rises initially from 70.27 in 2026 to a peak of 70.64 in 2028. However, after 2028, the index experiences a continuous downward decline, falling to 70.41 by 2030. The simulation indicates that unmitigated chemical fertilizer usage induces biophysical soil degradation (soil health declines from 0.65 to 0.58), creating a systemic limits-to-growth ceiling.

Under Scenario 2 (Economic Intervention), price supports and fertilizer subsidies elevate SFSI to 75.34 in 2026, reaching a peak of 75.62 in 2028, with a 7.13% increase relative to the Baseline scenario in 2030. However, the trajectory mirrors the baseline decay pattern after 2028, declining to 75.43 by 2030. Purely economic incentives fail to arrest physical soil health depletion.

Under Scenario 3 (Environmental Intervention), restricting chemical fertilizers and mandating organic transitions generates continuous, resilient growth (the SFSI increases from 77.03 in 2026 to 77.61 in 2030, representing a 10.23% increase relative to the Baseline scenario in 2030). Controlling agrochemical inputs breaks the reinforcing soil degradation loop (R1), enabling natural biophysical recovery.

Under Scenario 4 (Combined Policy Intervention), integrating price guarantees with organic transitions achieves the highest score (the SFSI reaches 81.12 in 2030, representing a 15.21% increase relative to the Baseline scenario). Scenario 4 combines immediate economic revenue protection with long-term ecological restoration.

sec.title: 5. Discussion
sec.p: The dynamic simulation results support the central working hypothesis of this study: evaluating staple crop food security solely through short-term economic protection (Profit) or volume availability (People) induces systemic limits-to-growth ceilings, whereas biophysical soil organic restoration (Planet) serves as a primary structural leverage point for long-term supply chain resilience.

sec.title: 5.1. Inter-agency decision trade-offs and hypothesis verification
sec.p: The comparative trajectories across Scenarios 1 to 4 provide actionable insights into operational trade-offs facing regional food governance. In evaluating pure economic stimulus (Scenario 2), upstream price supports managed by the National Food Agency under Regulation No. 04/2024 [32], alongside input subsidies allocated under Ministry of Agriculture Regulation No. 01/2024 [33], cogenerate an immediate financial buffer for farming households. However, the post-2028 trajectory flattening, during which the SFSI drops from 75.62 to 75.43 indicates that monetary stimulus alone cannot fully offset underlying physical soil degradation. Building on prior agroecosystem SD research [35], this study demonstrates that economic protectionism without ecological safeguards yields diminishing returns over multi-year horizons.

Conversely, biophysical soil restoration acts as a systemic leverage point, as observed in the Environmental Intervention (Scenario 3). Phasing chemical fertilizer caps alongside organic substitution, in alignment with decarbonization strategies and optimized bio-organic application frameworks [34], effectively breaks the reinforcing soil degradation loop (R1). Improving soil health restores crop yields naturally, thereby aligning with sustainable agriculture frameworks [10], [11], which emphasize that ecological carrying capacity forms an essential foundation for social accessibility and long-term farm income.

Resolving these inter-agency conflicts requires an integrated execution approach, as modeled in Scenario 4. The combined policy results indicate that economic incentives and environmental caps are not mutually exclusive strategies. By pairing minimum guaranteed purchase prices [32] with subsidized bio-organic fertilizer distribution and partial nitrogen substitution [34], decision-makers achieve SFSI Performance (= 81.12 by 2030). This integrated configuration addresses historical policy frictions between revenue-focused regulatory frameworks and long-term conservation mandates.

sec.title: 5.2. Implementation feasibility and transition management
sec.p: Translating the projected performance of Scenarios 3 and 4 into real-world execution requires managing critical operational friction points that lie outside pure differential equation models. Primary among these friction points is the biological time lag inherent in soil recovery, where biophysical soil organic matter regeneration typically requires a continuous 2–3-year application cycle. An abrupt 40% reduction in chemical fertilizers without sufficient organic transition buffers risks inducing short-term yield shocks and temporary farm income losses. Furthermore, scaling bio-organic inputs across 1.84 million hectares in East Java presents supply chain constraints, suggesting that regional authorities should establish localized composting facilities and bio-fertilizer processing centers to guarantee timely input delivery.

Beyond physical supply chain bottlenecks, farmer behavioral resistance and extension capacity represent notable social hurdles; smallholder farmers frequently resist reducing agrochemical inputs due to perceived yield risks. Overcoming this behavioral inertia requires expanding agricultural extension services and participatory farmer field schools to demonstrate organic efficacy. Finally, enforcing chemical fertilizer distribution quotas and verifying organic soil compliance introduces administrative monitoring overhead for regional supervisory commissions.

To systematically mitigate these transition risks, regional planners should adopt a phased three-stage execution roadmap. Phase 1 (years 1–2) focuses on pilot district demonstration and infrastructure development across major rice-producing centers (e.g., Mojokerto and Nganjuk), while expanding extension training programs, constructing regional organic processing units, and providing temporary financial cushions to buffer farmers during the transition. Subsequently, Phase 2 (years 3–4) enforces progressive chemical fertilizer quota reductions of 10–15% annually, strictly synchronized with the scaling and distribution of subsidized bio-organic fertilizers. Ultimately, Phase 3 (year 5 onward) achieves full regional policy integration across East Java, sustained by real-time digital soil health monitoring networks to support long-term ecological and economic stability.

sec.title: 5.3. Agency-specific action matrix and boundary limitations
sec.p: To ensure practical utility for decision-makers in engineering management, the operational responsibilities across regional food governance entities are structured around explicit inter-agency action mandates. Under this coordinated framework, the National Food Agency is responsible for conditioning minimum guaranteed purchase prices on farmer compliance with sustainable soil management practices [32]. Simultaneously, the Ministry of Agriculture must reallocate existing chemical fertilizer subsidy budgets toward scaling bio-organic supply chains and expanding agricultural extension training [33]. To complement these economic and technical measures, agricultural extension services and regional authorities are mandated to establish soil organic carbon monitoring networks, drive mandatory organic fertilizer substitution, and enforce broader agricultural decarbonization targets [34].

Despite these actionable insights, the validity and generalizability of these scenario projections remain strictly bounded by the structural scope of this study, as SD models are inherently tailored to their defined boundary conditions [27]. Geographically and temporally, the simulation model is calibrated exclusively for the regional rice supply chain of East Java, Indonesia, spanning a 2026–2030 simulation horizon. Furthermore, because the model focuses intentionally on upstream agricultural production and soil biophysical dynamics, it explicitly excludes downstream retail price volatility, interregional distribution logistics, extreme climate disruption shocks (such as severe El Niño events), and household-level micro-economics. Consequently, these quantitative findings should not be interpreted as direct empirical evidence for all agricultural regions in Indonesia or for other staple crops without prior recalibration of local biophysical, land-use, and demographic parameters.

sec.title: 6. Conclusions
sec.p: This study engineered and evaluated a TBL-based SD model to address rice food security governance in East Java, Indonesia. The simulation findings suggest that biophysical soil health restoration constitutes a critical leverage point required to mitigate limits-to-growth saturation in regional staple crop production. From an academic perspective, this research contributes to agricultural SD modeling by offering a quantitative framework that couples biophysical soil degradation formulations with TBL economic and social metrics.

Operationally, the results translate into a proposed agency-specific action matrix for regional food governance: the National Food Agency needs to align minimum guaranteed purchase prices with sustainable farming compliance; the Ministry of Agriculture should consider reallocating chemical fertilizer subsidies toward bio-organic supply chains and extension training; and the Ministry of Environment and Forestry is encouraged to enforce regional soil organic carbon monitoring alongside agricultural decarbonization targets.

However, the applicability of these scenario projections remains strictly bounded by the study’s structural scope, which focuses on East Java's upstream production dynamics through a 2026–2030 simulation horizon. Consequently, these model-based findings should not be directly generalized to agricultural regions with contrasting biophysical or logistical profiles without recalibrating local parameters. To expand upon these boundary conditions, future research should integrate downstream retail logistics, price volatility, and extreme climate disruption shocks.
